title: Should we still learn mental arithmetic?

turns.speaker: Josie
turns.text: My nephew can't do fourteen times six without reaching for a phone, and I can't decide whether that matters.

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: It matters for estimation, which is the thing nobody teaches explicitly. Knowing roughly what an answer should be.

turns.speaker: Erin
turns.text: That's the actual skill, yes. Not the calculation, the sense that a number is wrong.

turns.speaker: Josie
turns.text: You can have that without knowing tables, surely.

turns.speaker: Erin
turns.text: Less easily than you'd think. If fourteen sixes isn't somewhere near instant, you can't feel that eight hundred is absurd.

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: There's a working memory argument too. If the arithmetic takes all your attention, there's nothing left for the actual problem.

turns.speaker: Josie
turns.text: That one I find persuasive. It's why reading fluency matters even though you could sound out every word.

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: The counter is time. Every hour on tables is an hour not spent on reasoning or statistics, and statistics is what most adults actually need.

turns.speaker: Josie
turns.text: Massively more useful and barely taught.

turns.speaker: Erin
turns.text: Although you can't do statistics without number sense either, so it's not a clean trade.

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: So the answer is fluency to a point, and then stop, rather than drilling for four years.

turns.speaker: Erin
turns.text: Which is roughly what the evidence says and almost nowhere does.

points: The discussion concerns whether mental arithmetic still matters when calculators are available.
Tariq and Erin argue its value lies in estimation, the ability to sense that an answer is wrong.
Erin contends this requires near-instant recall of basic facts.
A working memory argument holds that slow arithmetic consumes attention needed for the actual problem, paralleling reading fluency.
Tariq notes the opportunity cost, since statistics is more useful for most adults and barely taught.
Erin replies statistics also requires number sense, and they conclude fluency should be developed to a point rather than drilled for years.
